title: Gandhi at Buckingham Palace: Clothes Enough for Both of Us!
summary: When reporters asked if he felt underdressed before the King Emperor, Gandhi famously quipped: 'The King had on enough clothes for both of us!'
keywords: Gandhi at Buckingham Palace: Clothes Enough for Both of Us!
full_text:
In the damp autumn of 1931, the city of London hosted the Second Round Table Conference to deliberate upon the political future of India. Attending as the sole representative of the Indian National Congress was Mahatma Gandhi.

During the proceedings, King Emperor George V invited conference delegates to an afternoon tea reception at Buckingham Palace.

Strict court protocol dictated formal morning dress: silk top hats, tailored morning coats, cravats, and polished leather shoes. Any departure from this etiquette was considered a grave insult to the Crown.

Winston Churchill and imperial hardliners expressed horror when rumors spread that the Indian leader intended to enter the palace in his usual attire. Churchill had already fulminated against the spectacle of a "half-naked seditious fakir striding half-naked up the steps of the Viceregal Palace."

Undeterred, Gandhi ascended the grand marble staircase of Buckingham Palace wearing his modest handspun khadi loincloth, a coarse cotton shawl draped across his shoulders, and simple leather sandals.

Inside the opulent hall, King George V stood adorned in gold epaulettes, diamond medals, and imperial robes. Gandhi greeted the monarch with folded hands and engaged in polite, candid conversation regarding Indian aspirations.

As Gandhi emerged through the palace gates, an army of international journalists surged forward with microphones and notebooks.

A British reporter asked with sly provocation:
"Mr. Gandhi! Did you not feel inappropriately dressed and terribly self-conscious attending upon His Majesty with so little clothing?"

Gandhi's eyes twinkled behind his round wire-rimmed spectacles. A radiant, childlike grin spread across his face as he replied softly:

**"Not at all, my friend! You see, the King Emperor had on enough clothes for both of us!"**

Laughter erupted among the press corps. The following morning, newspapers across Europe and America splashed Gandhi's brilliant repartee across their front pages.

By confronting imperial opulence with moral simplicity, Gandhi demonstrated that human dignity does not reside in velvet robes and gold braid, but in the purity of truth.
moral: True moral authority requires no ostentation; simplicity is the highest expression of authentic dignity.
witty_quote: The King had on enough clothes for both of us; so there was no shortage of apparel whatsoever!
